en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question of Inference.
1. The Question on Vessantara “Venerable Nāgasena, do all Bodhisattas give away their children and wives, or was it only by King Vessantara that his children and wife were given away?
“All Bodhisattas, O Great King, give away their children and wives; it was not only by King Vessantara that his children and wife were given away.”
“Moreover, venerable Nāgasena, she gave them with their consent.

“A wife, Great King, gives with her husband’s consent. But the children were crying out of their youth; had they understood the matter, they too would have given their consent and would not have cried out.
“It was difficult, venerable Nāgasena, what was done by the Bodhisatta, in that he gave his own dear sons, born of his own breast, to a brahmin for the sake of slavery.”

This too was a second thing more difficult than the difficult: that he looked on with equanimity when he saw his own dear, beloved young sons bound by a creeper and being rubbed by that brahmin with the creeper.

This too was a third thing more difficult than the difficult: that having freed himself from his bonds by his own strength, he gave back the children who had returned full of affection, having bound them again with a creeper.
This too was a fourth thing more difficult than the difficult: that he did not comfort the children who were crying out, "Father, this yakkha is taking us away to eat!
This too was a fifth thing more difficult than the difficult: that he fell at the feet of the weeping Prince Jāli and said, "Enough, father!
Turn back Kanhajina; I myself will go with the yakkha; let him eat me."
When he was thus entreating him, saying, "I am a *yakkha*," [Jāli] did not accept it.

This too is the sixth thing more difficult than the difficult: that while looking upon us who were suffering in the vast wilderness devoid of humans, he said to Prince Jāli, "Surely, dear one, your heart is like a stone, since you do not come to our aid."
He felt no compassion for him as he lamented, "The yakṣa is carrying him away, yet you do not stop him!
This too is the seventh thing more difficult than the difficult:

that when his son was being led away by that most terrifying and fearsome being until he vanished from sight, his heart did not shatter into a hundred or a thousand pieces—such is the case for a person who desires merit.
"What is the use of causing suffering to others? Should one not indeed give gifts oneself?
"Because he performed what was difficult to do, Great King, the fame of the Bodhisatta has resounded throughout the ten-thousandfold world system among gods and humans;
the devas proclaim it in the abode of the devas, and the asuras proclaim it in the abode of the asuras."
The garuḍas proclaim it in the garuḍa realm; the nāgas proclaim it in the nāga realm; the yakkhas proclaim it in the yakkha realm.
Gradually, by way of successive transmission, his fame has reached us here today at our assembly.
As we sit commemorating that gift, we wonder whether it was well-given or ill-given.
Moreover, Great King, this report of fame demonstrates ten qualities in Bodhisattvas who are skillful, wise, learned, and discerning.
What are these ten?
They are: freedom from pride, lack of attachment, generosity, relinquishment, non-returning, subtlety, greatness, and being difficult to comprehend.
“The rarity and incomparability of the Buddha-dhamma— this fame, O Great King,
proclaims these ten qualities to the skillful, the wise, the learned,
and the discerning Bodhisattvas. “Venerable Nāgasena, if one gives a gift after having caused suffering to another, does that gift still result in happiness and lead to rebirth in heaven?”
“Yes, Great King, what more can be said?
“Come now, venerable Nāgasena, please show me the reason.
“In this case, Great King, suppose there were some ascetic or brahmin who was virtuous and possessed of wholesome qualities; he might be...”
“Or suppose a man were crippled, or a cripple, or afflicted with some other disease;
and someone desiring merit were to place him in a vehicle and bring him to the place he desired— would there, Great King,
arise for that man any happiness on that account, and would that action lead to rebirth in heaven?”
“Yes, venerable sir, what could be said?
That man, venerable sir, might obtain an elephant-vehicle, or a horse-vehicle, or a chariot-vehicle; on land, a land-vehicle;
on water, a water-vehicle; among the gods, a divine vehicle; among humans, a human vehicle—suitable for that and conforming to that.”
"In birth after birth he would be reborn; there would arise for him pleasures appropriate and conducive to that state;
he would go from a happy destination to a happy destination; and by the very convergence of that karma, mounting upon psychic powers, he would reach the city of Nibbāna as he had aspired."
“Therefore, Great King, a gift given by causing suffering to others has a happy result and leads to heaven, such as the happiness that man experiences after having caused suffering to the oxen.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to another, further reason why a gift given by causing suffering to others has a happy result and leads to heaven.
Here, Great King, suppose some king, having collected lawful taxes from his realm, exercises his authority...”
“Suppose he were to give a gift, Great King—would that king, on account of that, experience any happiness conducive to rebirth in heaven?
“Yes, venerable sir; what need is there to say it? On account of that, venerable sir, that king would obtain many hundreds of thousands of times more merit.”

“He would be the supreme king among kings, the supreme god among gods, the supreme Brahmā among Brahmās, the supreme ascetic among ascetics, the supreme brahmin among brahmins, and the supreme Arhat among Arhats.

“In that case, Great King, a gift given by inflicting suffering upon others has a happy result and leads to heaven, since that king, having oppressed the people with force, experiences such superior glory and happiness through the gift he gave.”
“Excessive giving, venerable Nāgasena, was given by King Vessantara when he gave away his own wife to be another’s wife and gave away his own legitimate sons to be a brahmin’s slaves.
Excessive giving, venerable Nāgasena, is censured and condemned by the wise in the world; just as, venerable Nāgasena, [one is censured] for an excessive burden...”
The axle of a cart breaks; a ship sinks under excessive weight; food eaten in excess is digested improperly;
grain is destroyed by excessive rain; wealth is exhausted by excessive giving; the earth is scorched by excessive heat; one becomes insane through excessive passion;
one becomes liable to execution through excessive hatred; one falls into misfortune through excessive delusion; [one suffers] through excessive greed.
One enters a place where robbers are being seized; one is paralyzed by excessive fear; one crosses a river when it is too full;
lightning strikes due to an excessive wind; rice porridge overflows because of an excessive fire; and one does not live long due to excessive wandering.

In the same way, venerable Nāgasena, excessive giving is censured and condemned by the wise in the world. Venerable Nāgasena, that which was given by King Vessantara was excessive giving; no fruit whatsoever should be expected from it.”
“Excessive giving, O Great King, is praised, extolled, and lauded by the wise in the world; whoever gives any kind of gift whatsoever, the giver of excessive gifts attains fame in the world.
Just as, O Great King, a divine forest-root, because of its extreme excellence, does not reveal itself even when grasped and held in the hand of others standing nearby;
or as a medicinal elixir, because of its superior nature, eradicates affliction and brings an end to diseases; or as fire, because of its intense radiance...”
Fire burns; water extinguishes by its extreme coolness; the lotus, due to its purity, is not defiled by water or mud;
the jewel, due to its supreme quality, grants desires; the diamond, due to its extreme sharpness, pierces gems, pearls, and crystals;
the earth, due to its vastness, supports humans, serpents, wild animals, birds, water, stones, mountains, and trees; and the ocean, due to its vastness...
Sineru is immovable because it is not filled to capacity; space is infinite because it is exceedingly vast; the sun destroys darkness because of its excessive brilliance;
the lion is free from fear because of his noble birth; the wrestler quickly throws down his opponent because of his great strength;
the king is a sovereign because of his great merit; and the monk is [unassailable] by nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and devas because of his extreme virtue.
The Buddha is worthy of homage, peerless because of his supreme excellence.
In the same way, Great King, that which is called "the supreme gift" is praised, extolled, and lauded by the wise in the world.
Whatever kind of gift anyone may give, the giver of the supreme gift attains fame in the world; through the supreme gift, Vessantara—
"King, you have been praised, extolled, lauded, honored, and celebrated throughout the ten-thousandfold world system because of that very same excessive giving;
for that reason, King Vessantara has now become a Buddha, the foremost in the world with its devas.
But, Great King, is there any gift in the world that should be set aside—a gift that ought not to be given when a worthy recipient has arrived?"
“Furthermore, venerable Nāgasena, there are these ten gifts that are considered non-gifts in the world; whoever gives those gifts goes to the states of misery.
What are the ten?
Venerable Nāgasena, the gift of liquor is considered a non-gift in the world; whoever gives that gift goes to the states of misery.”
The gift of a thoroughbred horse …pe… the gift of a woman … the gift of a bull …
The gift of mental action … the gift of weapons … the gift of poison …
The gift of shackles...
the gift of chickens and pigs...
the gift of false weights and false measures, venerable Nāgasena, is considered in the world to be no gift at all; he who gives such a gift goes to a state of misery.
“Venerable Nāgasena, these ten kinds of gifts are indeed considered non-gifts in the world; whoever gives such gifts goes to a state of misery.

“I do not ask you, Great King, about what is considered a non-gift. Rather, this is what I ask you, Great King: ‘Is there, Great King, in the world any gift that should be withheld, which ought not to be given when a worthy recipient has arrived?
“There is no gift in the world, Venerable Nāgasena, that should be withheld.”
When those worthy of offerings have arrived, there is nothing that should not be given. When faith has arisen in the mind, some give food to those worthy of offerings,
some clothing, some bedding, some dwellings, some rugs and coverlets,
some male and female slaves, some fields and lands, some bipeds and quadrupeds, and some hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands.
“Some give away their great kingdom, and some even their very lives.
“But if, Great King, some even give away their lives, for what reason did you so excessively harass Vessantara, the lord of givers, regarding his son Sudinna and his wife?
Is there not, Great King, a worldly custom, a worldly practice, whereby a father who is burdened by debt or driven by the need for a livelihood may lend or sell his son?”
“Yes, venerable sir, a father may, when he is burdened by debt or driven by the need for a livelihood,
hand over his son or sell him. “If, great king, a father may indeed hand over or sell his son when he is burdened by debt or driven by the need for a livelihood,
then King Vessantara, O great king, being unable to attain omniscience and being thus afflicted and distressed— ”
“For the sake of acquiring the wealth of the Dhamma, he gave away and even sold his wife and children.
Thus, Great King, Vessantara the king gave only what was rightfully his to give, and did only what was rightfully his to do.
Why then, Great King, do you so vehemently revile Vessantara, the lord of givers, for that act of giving?”
“Venerable Nāgasena, I do not criticize the generosity of the Lord of Giving, Vessantara; however, when asked for his wife and children, he should have given himself instead.

“This, Great King, is an improper course of action—that one should give oneself when asked for wife and children. Whatever is asked for, that very thing should be given; this is the practice of true men.
Suppose, Great King, some man were to ask for water, and another man were to give him food—would that man, Great King, have fulfilled the other’s request?”
“Certainly not, Bhante; one who gives him exactly what he has asked for would be doing his duty.
“In the same way, Great King, King Vessantara gave his children and wife to the brahmins when they asked for them.
If, Great King, a brahmin were to ask for Vessantara’s own body, he would not protect himself, nor would he waver or feel attachment; his body would simply be given and relinquished.”
If, O Great King, someone were to approach the donor Vessantara and ask, "Become my slave," his body would indeed have been given and relinquished;
having given it, he would not regret it. For the body of King Vessantara, O Great King, was common to many.
Just as, Great King, a piece of cooked meat is common property to many,
even so, Great King, the body of King Vessantara was common property to many.
Or again, Great King, just as a tree bearing fruit is common property to various flocks of birds;
In the same way, Great King, King Vessantara’s body was shared by many.
For what reason?
Because he thought: “By practicing in this manner, I shall attain perfect enlightenment.”
Just as, great king, a poor man seeking wealth, wandering in search of riches, travels along goat paths, bramble paths, and cane paths;
he engages in trade by sea and by land; he acquires wealth through body, speech, and mind;
and he exerts himself for the sake of obtaining wealth.
In the same way, Great King, the lord of generosity Vessantara, though himself poor in worldly wealth, gave away his money, grain, male and female slaves,
vehicles, draft animals, his entire estate, his own children and wife, and even himself to supplicants, all for the sake of obtaining the jewel of omniscience—
the wealth of a Buddha— and sought only perfect self-enlightenment.

Or again, Great King, just as a minister who desires the art of calculation (*muddā*) exerts himself to obtain that skill even by giving away whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold he has in his house;
even so, Great King, Vessantara the lord of givers, having given away all that external and internal wealth and even his own life to others, seeks only for perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

Moreover, Great King, it occurred to the generous Vessantara: “Whatever that brahmin asks for, by giving that very thing to him, I shall be one who fulfills his duty. Thus he gave away his children and wife.

It was not out of a desire to be stingy, Great King, that the generous Vessantara gave away his children and wife; nor did he give away his children and wife because he wished them no longer to see him;
nor did he give away his children and wife thinking, “I have too many children and a wife, and I am unable to support them. [Rather,] he gave away his children and wife.
It was not out of dissatisfaction or a desire to cast them out because they were "unpleasant" that he gave away his wife and children;
rather, it was solely because of his love for the jewel of omniscience and for the sake of omniscience that King Vessantara gave this incomparable,
vast, unsurpassed, dear, agreeable, beloved, and life-like gift of his wife and children to the brahmin.
This was also spoken, O Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above Gods, in the Cariyāpiṭaka:
“Neither both my sons are to be given away,
nor is Queen Maddī to be given away.”
"Omniscience is dear to me;
therefore, I gave what was dear.
Thus, Great King, after King Vessantara had given away his children as a gift, he entered the leaf-hut and lay down.
Because he was so deeply distressed, a powerful sorrow arose within him and his heart grew hot.
Unable to breathe through his nose, he emitted hot sighs and gasps through his mouth; his tears welled up and, turning into drops of blood, issued from his eyes.
In this very way, Great King, out of suffering, King Vessantara gave away his children and wife to the brahmin, thinking, "May my path of giving not diminish."
Moreover, Great King, King Vessantara gave his two children to the brahmin for two reasons.
What are these two?
"My path of giving shall not be abandoned," and "On account of this, my noble grandfather will release my two suffering children by means of forest roots and fruits."

For King Vessantara, Great King, knew: “It is not possible for anyone to consume my children as the property of a slave; moreover, my grandfather will ransom these children, and thus our departure will come to pass.
It was with these two purposes in mind, Great King, that he gave the two children to the brahmin.
Furthermore, Great King, King Vessantara knew: “This brahmin is aged, decrepit, and advanced in years.”
“[He is] weak, broken, dependent on a staff, his lifespan exhausted, and his merit meager; he is not capable of enjoying these children as the property of a slave.

“But could a man, O Great King, by means of his natural strength, seize the sun and moon—so powerful and so majestic—and, having placed them in a box or a basket, deprive them of their radiance and enjoy them as food from a platter?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, it is impossible for anyone to enjoy the children of Vessantara—who are like the sun and moon in this world—as slaves or property.
Furthermore, great king, hear another further reason why it is impossible for anyone to enjoy the children of Vessantara as slaves or property.”
Just as, great king, the jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch— beautiful, of noble birth, eight-faceted, well-polished,
four cubits in length, and as wide as a wagon hub— could not be wrapped in a piece of cloth, placed inside a box,
and used for the purpose of cutting or sharpening;
In the same way, Great King, no one is able to enjoy the children of Vessantara—who is like the jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch—as a slave-possessing.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why the children of Vessantara cannot be enjoyed by anyone as a slave-possessing:
just as, Great King, there is a horse that is all-white, marked with three white stripes, standing on seven limbs, eighteen cubits in height, and nine cubits in length and girth.
"Gracious and beautiful to behold, O Great King, the Naga king Uposatha cannot be covered over by anyone with a mere cloth or a bowl,
nor can he be kept confined like a calf in a calf-pen;
even so, O Great King, the children of Vessantara— who resemble the Naga king Uposatha— cannot be enjoyed as slaves by anyone in this world."
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why the children of Vessantara cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.

Just as, Great King, the great ocean—long, broad, vast, deep, immeasurable, difficult to cross, unfathomable, and unconfined—cannot be covered everywhere and enjoyed from a single landing-place by anyone;
even so, Great King, the children of Vessantara, who are like the great ocean in the world, cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why Vessantara’s children cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.

Just as, Great King, Himavanta, the king of mountains, rises five hundred yojanas into the sky, has a length and breadth of three thousand yojanas, is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, is the source of five hundred great rivers, and is the abode of a vast multitude of beings; so too, Great King, are these children.
Bearing various kinds of fragrances and adorned with hundreds of divine medicinal herbs, he appears rising high into the sky like a cloud;
even so, Great King, the children of Vessantara—who resembles the Himalaya, king of mountains—cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why the children of Vessantara cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.
"Just as, Great King, a great mass of fire burning on the summit of a mountain at night during the pitch-black darkness is visible even from a great distance;
even so, Great King, King Vessantara is manifest and visible even from afar like a great mass of fire burning on a mountain peak, and his children cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another reason why the children of Vessantara cannot be enjoyed by anyone as slaves or property."
Just as, Great King, when the *nāgapuppha* flowers bloom on the Himavat mountain and a straight wind blows, the fragrance of the flowers wafts for ten or twelve *yojanas*; even so, Great King,
the fame of King Vessantara has spread even across thousands of *yojanas*, as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, throughout the abodes of the *asuras*,
*garuḷas*, *gandhabbas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *mahoragas*, *kinnaras*, and *indras*.
The sublime fragrance of his excellent virtue wafted abroad; because of that, no one was able to consume his children as if they were slaves or property.
Your Majesty, Prince Jālī was thus instructed by his father, King Vessantara:
"Dear son, your grandfather is ransoming you from the brahmin by giving him wealth; let him ransom you by paying those thousand coins for the black antelope skin."

"Let him buy you back by paying a hundred slaves, a hundred slave-girls, a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred cows, a hundred bulls, and a hundred gold coins—that is, by giving all these hundreds.

If, dear son, your grandfather were to seize you from the hand of the brahmin by command and by force, for nothing at all, do not act upon your grandfather’s word; remain instead as followers of the brahmin alone."
"Let it be so," he instructed, and sent his sons away. Then Prince Jālī went and, being questioned by his grandfather, spoke:
"My father, dear grandfather, gave me to the brahmin for a price of a thousand pieces."
“And furthermore, a black antelope skin, a maiden,
and a hundred elephants.
“Well analyzed, venerable Nāgasena, is this question.”
The web of views has been torn asunder;
the doctrines of others have been thoroughly crushed;
one's own doctrine has been well illuminated.
"The phrasing is perfectly purified;
the meaning is well-expounded;
thus it is, and so do I accept it."
The First Question of Vessantara.
